items.title: Can My Homemade AC Run Off Grid? Here’s How Much Power It Uses
items.description: - OUPES Guardian 6000 V2: https://tidd.ly/4xBsjI1 - 5% Discount Code: CRAFTSMANCHRIS How much power does my homemade AC/heat pump actually use — and can I run the entire thing off grid? Catch up on the video series here. Part 1 - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RhgFEHgjPqY&t=6s Part 2 - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-ee1ZWDiVdQ&t=25s Part 3 - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GfMNLWzaUHU&t=192s ▶️ Full DIY Geothermal Playlist: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RhgFEHgjPqY&list=PLDZoJOo-bEnA In this video, I put my DIY geothermal-style AC system to the test using the OUPES Guardian 6000 V2. This system started life as a window air conditioner, but I’ve completely changed the way it rejects heat by using water and my homemade ground-loop setup instead of the original outdoor condenser. This time, I wanted to look at the electrical side of the project. I measure how much power the homemade AC actually pulls while it’s running, then see what happens when I disconnect from the grid and power it with the Guardian 6000 V2. But I didn’t stop with the AC. I also put the Guardian to work around my **barn and house** to see how practical a large portable power station like this actually is for the type of projects and backup-power situations I deal with around my property. The goal wasn’t just to see whether it could turn everything on. I wanted to get a better understanding of how much energy these loads actually consume, how long a battery system could realistically power them, and what it would take to operate more of my property without depending entirely on the grid. My homemade AC project is still an experiment, and there’s plenty more testing and improving to come. But being able to measure the power consumption and actually run the system off grid is another big step forward. If you’ve been following the DIY geothermal project, there’s a lot more coming as I continue improving the ground loop, controls, efficiency, and overall system. items.title: Turning a Dumpster AC Into a Super-Efficient Geothermal Heat Pump
items.description: Part 3 of my DIY geothermal AC project is finally here. In this video, I take a free **14,000 BTU LG Dual Inverter window air conditioner** that I pulled out of a dumpster and turn it into a homemade ground-source cooling system. Catch up on the video series here. Part 1 - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RhgFEHgjPqY&t=1s Part 2 - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-ee1ZWDiVdQ&t=24s Part 3 - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ntVCKMdNUj0&t=1s Part 4 - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VfJH4ksIz2I&t=156s Part 5 - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j6oyHpL8w70&t=134s ▶️ Full DIY Geothermal Playlist: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RhgFEHgjPqY&list=PLDZoJOo-bEnA&pp=sAgC I cleaned the unit up, removed the condenser fan, rotated the condenser without opening the refrigerant circuit, built a water jacket around it, and tied it into my 2,000 feet of buried PEX ground loop. The idea is simple: instead of dumping heat into hot outside air, the AC rejects that heat into circulating ground-loop water. By the end of the test, I was seeing very cold air making it upstairs into the main living space. This project has changed a lot since the beginning, and a big part of that has come from your comments, suggestions, questions, and ideas. items.title: 1 Month With My Homemade Geothermal AC System — Here’s How It’s Doing
items.description: It’s officially been one month since I fired up my homemade DIY geothermal AC system, so it’s time to see how it’s actually performing. Catch up on the video series here. Part 1 - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RhgFEHgjPqY&t=1s Part 2 - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-ee1ZWDiVdQ&t=24s Part 3 - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ntVCKMdNUj0&t=1s Part 4 - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VfJH4ksIz2I&t=156s For this project, I buried roughly 2,000 feet of pipe in the ground and built a closed-loop system designed to use the naturally cooler ground temperature to help cool my house. After weeks of digging, plumbing, wiring, testing, troubleshooting, and making adjustments, I finally got the system running. Now that it’s had a full month of real-world use, I’m checking the water temperatures, airflow, system performance, and overall results to see if this crazy DIY geothermal experiment is actually worth it. In this video I’ll show you how the system has been holding up, what I’ve learned so far, what I would change, and whether I’m still happy with the results. If you haven’t watched Parts 1 and 2 yet, go back and check those out to see how the entire system was built from the ground up. This project is experimental and based on my own DIY setup and experience. Always do your own research and follow applicable electrical, plumbing, HVAC, and building codes. items.title: The Truth About Owning an Outdoor Wood Boiler
items.description: After one full year of heating with an outdoor wood boiler, I’ve learned a LOT — and there are definitely a few things I wish I knew before I started. In this video, I’m sharing 5 of the biggest lessons I learned during my first year of owning and operating a wood boiler. From burning wood and keeping the fire going to maintenance, efficiency, and some of the little things nobody really tells you about, these are the things I think every new or future wood boiler owner should know. Overall, I’ve really enjoyed heating with wood, but there’s definitely more to owning an outdoor wood boiler than just throwing a few logs in the firebox! If you already heat with a wood boiler, let me know in the comments: What’s one thing YOU wish you knew when you first started? And if you’re considering installing one, drop your questions below. I’ll do my best to answer them based on what I’ve learned so far. Thanks for watching! items.title: I Have a Crazy Heat Pump Idea... Will It Actually Work?
items.description: I've had this idea stuck in my head for a while, and before I start cutting, welding, and building... I want your opinion. Can an old window air conditioner be turned into a DIY water chiller for a hydronic cooling system? The goal is to cool water instead of air and use it with a heat exchanger to cool my house. On paper, it seems possible—but there are a lot of questions. Can the refrigerant system handle it? Would the efficiency be worth it? What problems am I overlooking? In this video, I tear down an old window AC unit, explain the concept, and walk through my plan. Now I'm turning it over to you. 💬 Would this actually work? 💬 What challenges do you see? 💬 Have you ever built something similar? I read the comments, and your feedback often shapes the projects I build next. If enough people think this has potential, there's a good chance you'll see me build it.
